analysis.one_liner: Repeals all corporate income taxes and estate taxes and taxes only wages at 10%.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee and expired when the Congress ended in January 1991, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have eliminated the corporate income tax, the estate and gift taxes, and taxes on insurance companies, mutual funds, real estate trusts, and foreign corporations doing business in the United States. It would have replaced the individual income tax with a flat 10% tax on wages and self-employment earnings above $10,000 a year, while leaving investment income such as capital gains, dividends, interest, and rents completely untaxed. It would also have wiped out every individual tax deduction and credit, including the standard deduction and the Earned Income Tax Credit.
analysis.who_benefits: Large corporations and their shareholders, wealthy households, and the specific industries named in the bill — insurance companies, mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, and foreign investors — would pay dramatically less tax. Wealthy families would escape estate and gift taxes entirely, and anyone living off investments rather than a paycheck would owe no income tax at all.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the corporate income tax, the corporate alternative minimum tax, and taxes on insurance companies, mutual savings banks, regulated investment companies, and real estate investment trusts [S2] [S3].
It repeals the estate tax, the gift tax, and the generation-skipping transfer tax, so large inherited fortunes would pass tax-free [S2] [S3].

It taxes only 'earned income' — wages, salaries, and self-employment earnings — above a $10,000 exemption, leaving capital gains, dividends, interest, and rental income outside the tax base [S2] [S3].
It also repeals the tax on foreign corporations' U.S.-connected income [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Working people. Because only earnings from work would be taxable, the entire individual income tax burden would fall on paychecks. A worker earning $60,000 would owe 10% of everything above $10,000 — $5,000 — while an investor living off dividends and capital gains would owe nothing. The bill also eliminates every deduction and credit, removing the standard deduction, the Earned Income Tax Credit, the child credit, and the mortgage interest deduction. The bill does not say how it would replace the hundreds of billions in revenue lost from repealing corporate and estate taxes.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals all individual tax deductions and credits, which would end the standard deduction, the Earned Income Tax Credit, the child tax credit, and the mortgage interest deduction [S2] [S3].

Repealing the corporate income tax, estate and gift taxes, and taxes on insurance companies and investment vehicles would remove a very large share of federal revenue, and the bill provides no replacement funding [S2].

Because only earned income is taxed, a flat 10% levy on wages would shift the tax burden away from wealth and investment income and onto work, so someone living off investments would pay nothing while a worker earning the same amount would pay [S3].
The bill relies on the Treasury to draft all necessary conforming changes within 90 days, leaving the basic structure of the new tax system undefined at enactment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain would go overwhelmingly to corporations, investors, and large estates; the cost would fall on workers, whose paychecks would become the tax base, and on whatever programs Congress would later have to cut or debt it would have to issue to replace the lost revenue. Low-wage workers under the $10,000 exemption would pay less, but middle-income workers would lose deductions and credits that currently reduce their bills.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Helms introduced the bill, the Senate sent it to the Finance Committee, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Jesse Helms of North Carolina introduced the Tithe Tax Act of 1989 on February 22, 1989 [S1] [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; no further action was ever taken [S1] [S5].
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill expired in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, corporations, large estates, and investment income kept paying the taxes it would have repealed, and wage earners were spared a tax system that would have placed the entire income tax burden on their paychecks while eliminating deductions and credits.

for.name: Sen. Jesse Helms
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Tithe Tax Act of 1989 in the Senate on February 22, 1989.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 22, 1989 and never scheduled a markup or reported it out, letting it expire.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough to reveal a partisan split: it had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no votes were ever taken [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have repealed the corporate income tax and corporate minimum tax entirely, eliminating a major source of federal revenue. The cost would have shifted to workers through either higher taxes on wages or cuts to public programs.

industries.industry: Insurance companies, mutual funds, and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill names these industries specifically for repeal of their special taxes, so they would have paid nothing on their income.

industries.industry: Foreign corporations doing business in the U.S.
industries.note: The tax on foreign corporations' U.S.-connected income would have been repealed, putting them on equal footing with domestic firms at no domestic cost.
Repeal of estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes would have let large inheritances pass tax-free, and untaxed investment income would have removed most tax on the wealthy.

industries.industry: Tax preparers and tax software industry
industries.note: A wage-only tax with no deductions, credits, or exclusions would have simplified filing dramatically and reduced demand for professional tax preparation and complex planning.
